events.excerpt: Author: HyperLend Team Date: 2026-11-06 Summary This proposal seeks Aave DAO recognition of a new HyperLend deployment as a friendly fork of Aave, on Elysium, Kinetiq’s Layer 2 for the Hyperliquid ecosystem. The deployment will use the Aave v3.7 codebase and will consist only of Aave pools. HyperLend will share 50% of all revenue generated by the Elysium deployment with the Aave DAO. The remaining 50% will be used to buy back HyperLend’s token, HPL. Block Analitica will continue to serve as risk manager. Motivation HyperLend’s track record In early 2025, the Aave DAO recognized HyperLend as a friendly fork on HyperEVM ( TEMP CHECK , ARFC ). Since then, HyperLend has: Originated approximately $2B in loans ( Block Analitica dashboard ) Reached a peak total market size of over $900M ( Block Analitica dashboard ), and currently holds over $530M in TVL with $250M in active loans ( DefiLlama ) Operated securely and at scale for more than a year Worked continuously with Block Analitica on risk management We believe this record shows HyperLend can run an Aave-based money market responsibly. We want to bring that experience to a second network. Why Elysium Elysium is a high-throughput Arbitrum Orbit L2 built by Kinetiq. It settles to HyperEVM, runs co-located with HyperCore, and uses HYPE

events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. On every unlock the extension calls fetchJettonInfo() . Jettons are TON tokens,

events.excerpt: Hi all. We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. The motivator was Anthropic’s recent work on zero-knowledge proofs of LLM inference . The Solana drafts and the discussion so far: Overview and drafts: Bringing Inference Programs To Solana Microsite with diagrams and a sandbox: asc.verafy.ai Discussion: solana-improvement-documents #724 We have no strong view on whether this is technically feasible, and we know there is a lot of prior work here that we may not have accounted for, including optimistic oracles and opML. The drafts were written with help from AI tools, so some of it may be poorly reasoned. The questions we’d most like help with: Is this better as an application-level ERC, or not a standard at all? events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwa
events.headline: ERC-8486: Flash Loan Proxy

events.excerpt: Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system
events.headline: Stealth ABBE over BLS12-381: Zero-Metadata Broadcast of Private Contracts & Encrypted State via EIP-4844 Blobs

events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.headline: EIP-8484: SLOTDURATION Opcode

That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it. events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. There was a bug present that did not follow this behavior in certain circumstances. The issue was first reported to Parity through its

events.excerpt: TL;DR: XCMv3 will be removed in polkadot-sdk stable2612 (release 2026-12-17, ingestion by fellowship runtimes only after that). Once system chains upgrade, they will no longer send or accept v3 messages. If your chain or your app still uses v3, you need to move to v4 or v5 before then. Check your chain on the dashboard: XCM Versions . XCMv5 was merged in November 2024: XCM v5 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #4826 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub . A PR removing v3 ( Remove XCMv3 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #13629 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub ) will ship in stable2612 , scheduled for 2026-12-17 . After that, system parachains and any other runtime can adopt it. Allowing for runtime releases and governance, expect the first chains to drop v3 in early 2027. Once a chain drops v3, it can’t decode v3 messages sent to it and can’t downgrade outgoing messages to v3. XCM between that chain and any other chain still on v3 will fail. events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release. events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release. events.excerpt: A Kusama Wish for Change needs a 666.67 KSM decision deposit before it can go to a vote. Governance takes that deposit from one account. A proposal can have support and still time out because nobody can carry the whole amount. We have built a contract that lets people and groups share it. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. Paseo rehearsal : free test PAS. Source, tests and logs . Verified Kusama contract . How it works Each pool is fixed to one referendum and its exact deposit. It has no owner, admin key or upgrade path. People contribute from their own accounts. The payment that fills the pool tries to place the deposit in the same transaction. If placement fails, the contribution stays in the pool and anyone can retry. Contributors can withdraw while the pool remains open, before placement. After the referendum ends, anyone can reclaim the deposit and send payouts to the contributing accounts. These are separate contract calls. No watcher is runnin

events.excerpt: Disclaimer: This is an independent proposal from an ordinary Cosmos community member. I am not affiliated with Cosmos Labs, the Interchain Foundation, or the Cosmos Hub development team. This is not an official initiative or a finalized technical specification. My intention is to share an idea and gather community feedback. TL;DR I would like to propose exploring ATOM Shield , a limited emergency freezing mechanism for native ATOM on the Cosmos Hub. The goal is to prevent stolen ATOM from being moved further during major security incidents, without halting the entire network, while leaving final decisions to decentralized governance. The proposed mechanism would work as follows: 1 Security Council member: Initiates an immediate freeze lasting up to 1 hour. Additional Council approval: Extends the freeze for up to 24 hours from the initial action. At least 2/3 of all active Council members within 24 hours: Confirms the freeze until governance reaches a decision. Cosmos Hub governance: Decides whether to unfreeze, maintain the freeze, or authorize recovery of the assets. Failure to meet approval thresholds: Results in automatic unfreezing.
